claims.text: Enhanced high-entropy stabilization governs the ability of near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles to maintain structural and chemical integrity at high temperature.
The initial nanoparticles are well-mixed, near-equiatomic, and single-phase solid solutions.
Conventional fabrication methods yield uniform solid-solution nanoparticles.
The intervention introduces controlled compositional gradients while retaining similar overall elemental ratios.
Catalytic tests will cover 773–1173 K and thermoelectric tests will cover 473–1923 K in reactive and inert atmospheres.
A uniform, near-equiatomic solid solution has high configurational mixing entropy.
High mixing entropy minimizes atomic mobility at elevated temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses high-temperature phase segregation.
A uniform, near-equiatomic elemental distribution maximizes configurational entropy.
Entropic stabilization reduces atomic diffusion pathways that would otherwise cause phase segregation or precipitation.
Suppressing diffusion-driven segregation or precipitation preserves nanoparticle structural integrity and chemical uniformity.
Uniform near-equiatomic nanoparticles will undergo less phase and compositional change during high-temperature operation than gradient-containing nanoparticles.
Uniform near-equiatomic nanoparticles will maintain high catalytic and thermoelectric performance during high-temperature operation.
Engineered compositional gradients will increase phase segregation.
Increased phase segregation will degrade catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to particles with intrinsic ordering or substantially different phase structures.
Direct causal evidence linking high-entropy stabilization to suppressed high-temperature segregation has not been established in the literature.
Failure of gradient-containing particles to show statistically greater segregation or performance degradation than uniform particles would falsify the hypothesis.
